intro: Oiseaux tristes (Très lent) is the second piece of Ravel’s Miroirs. It opens on a high B♭ alone, and the bird calls sound above slow piano figures, with a brief flurry in the middle.

sections.label: A · Solitary call on B♭, très lent
sections.mNote: The upper call begins without accompaniment.

sections.label: B · E major, calls and echoes
sections.mNote: Louder calls are echoed more softly over the moving left hand.

sections.label: A′ · The call returns in D minor
sections.mNote: The short–long call returns above held chords.

sections.label: Cadenza · Runs without bar lines
sections.mNote: The pianist stretches the rising and falling figures.

sections.label: Link · Three measured bars
sections.mNote: The original tempo returns and stops on a fermata.

sections.label: Coda · Low E♭, bird calls
sections.mNote: Slower still; the piano returns to E♭ minor.

cues.title: Opening, unaccompanied B♭
cues.text: A high B♭ repeats very softly, then turns into a short flourish. The left hand rests for three bars. When it enters, its quavers move in threes against the upper part’s twos.
cues.evidence: Miroirs, Demets edition (1906), p. 10: opening B♭, left-hand rests and simultaneous 4/4 and 12/8. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/e2/IMSLP02693-Ravel-Miroirs,DemetsEd.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, Paris, 1906
cues.text: Oiseaux tristes is dedicated to Ricardo Viñes. On 6 January 1906, at the Salle Érard in Paris, he gave the first performance of all five Miroirs.
cues.evidence: Dedication, première date, venue and pianist: https://imslp.org/wiki/Miroirs,_M.43_(Ravel,_Maurice).

cues.title: Enharmonic change to E major
cues.text: E♭ is rewritten as D♯, the same piano key, and the music moves to E major. A rolled chord opens a fuller passage. High calls sound forte and are then repeated softly, marked lointain (far away).
cues.evidence: Demets edition, pp. 10–11: four-sharp signature, rolled chord and f/pp calls. The E♭–D♯ reinterpretation is described at https://enc.piano.or.jp/en/musics/329.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ravel on Oiseaux tristes
cues.text: In dictated notes, Ravel called Oiseaux tristes the first of the five pieces in date and, in his view, the most typical. He described it as “birds lost in the torpor of a very dark forest in the hottest hours of summer”.
cues.evidence: Ravel’s notes dictated to Roland-Manuel, 10 October 1928 (BnF, Gallica btv1b10073212x, sheets 6–7): “Le premier en date de ces morceaux et le plus typique de tous est à mon sens le second du recueil: les Oiseaux tristes”, and on the next sheet “des oiseaux perdus dans la torpeur d’une forêt très sombre aux heures les plus chaudes de l’été”. Our translation. Roger Nichols quotes the same image: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W5434_67731

cues.title: Unbarred cadenza
cues.text: Ravel drops the bar lines for a cadenza. Slurred runs climb and turn over a slower line in the bass. The marking is Lent, presque ad lib., and even the fastest notes stay at ppp.
cues.evidence: Demets edition, p. 13, first three systems: unbarred cadenza, Lent, presque ad lib. and ppp.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing section in E♭ minor
cues.text: The music returns to E♭ minor over a low held E♭. Ravel marks the passage Encore plus lent, sombre et lointain (dark and distant). Short calls sound above the bass and fade under perdendo.
cues.evidence: Demets edition, p. 13, final system: six-flat signature, low E♭, Encore plus lent, sombre et lointain and perdendo.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: E♭ respelled as D♯ for E major
transitions.from: A · Solitary call on B♭, très lent
transitions.to: B · E major, calls and echoes
transitions.how: A short 2/4 bar closes the opening section. E♭ is respelled as D♯, the leading note of E major, and four sharps replace six flats. A rolled right-hand chord, marked expressif, sounds over a low held bass. Rising left-hand notes follow.
transitions.evidence: Demets edition (1906), pp. 10–11; harmonic reading: https://enc.piano.or.jp/en/musics/329.

transitions.title: The call returns above held chords
transitions.from: B · E major, calls and echoes
transitions.to: A′ · The call returns in D minor
transitions.how: The fast chords subside and Ravel writes revenez au mouvement. A one-flat key signature brings D minor. The opening’s short–long call returns above tied chords, with the pedal held.
transitions.evidence: Demets edition, p. 12: return to the original tempo, one-flat signature, held pedal and returning call.

transitions.title: Into the unbarred cadenza
transitions.from: A′ · The call returns in D minor
transitions.how: A short 2/4 bar leads into Lent, presque ad lib. The piano stays at ppp with the pedal held down. From here the runs are written without bar lines. Below the repeating right-hand figures, the left hand plays a slower melody.
transitions.evidence: Demets edition, pp. 12–13: 2/4 bar and unbarred cadenza.

transitions.title: Return to the opening tempo
transitions.how: The cadenza pushes slightly ahead, then au mouvement brings back the original tempo and the bar lines. A rising left-hand figure leads to a held chord beneath a short phrase in the upper part. Over three bars the dynamic grows from p to mf and falls back, and the passage ends under a fermata.
transitions.evidence: Demets edition, p. 13, third and fourth systems.

transitions.title: A low E♭ beneath the birds
transitions.how: After the fermata the six-flat signature returns. A low E♭ holds the piano in E♭ minor while the calls in the upper register are played slowly and softly. Ravel marks Encore plus lent, then perdendo over the last phrases.
transitions.evidence: Demets edition, p. 13, last two systems.

facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; Fauré for composition, André Gedalge for counterpoint
Ricardo Viñes · Maurice Delage · Tristan Klingsor · M. D. Calvocoressi
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber and piano music; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: To M. D. Calvocoressi, recalled in his Musicians Gallery (1933)

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery, and his mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He went back to the Basque coast many times. Spain appears often in his music, in the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera in the Rapsodie espagnole and the clocks of a Toledo clockmaker’s shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. André Gedalge gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and in January 1898 he entered the composition class of Fauré. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces he could not have played himself with comparable command.
